      "category": "Shared state and lifetime",
      "question": "How long must events and reservations persist, and across which people, devices, sessions, or service instances must they be shared?",
      "changes": "Storage design, deployment assumptions, and persistence tests.",
      "route": "default",
      "default": "Share state among callers of one running service instance, keep it in memory, and discard it when the process stops; sharing across instances and survival across restarts are out of scope.",

      "id": "Q3",
      "category": "Reservation behavior",
      "question": "How many seats does a reservation claim, and what should happen when capacity is exhausted or requests arrive concurrently?",
      "changes": "Reservation rules, concurrency handling, and capacity tests.",
      "route": "default",

      "blocks": "nothing: the default proceeds"

      "id": "Q4",
      "category": "HTTP interface",
      "question": "What HTTP interface and event information should callers use?",
      "changes": "Request and response formats, validation, and API tests.",
      "route": "default",
      "default": "Use a minimal JSON HTTP API that creates an event from a positive seat count, returns an event identifier, and accepts a reservation for that identifier; report invalid input, unknown events, and exhausted capacity with appropriate HTTP errors.",
      "blocks": "nothing: the default proceeds"
    },
    {
      "id": "Q5",
      "category": "Runtime and tests",
      "question": "What Python runtime, dependencies, and test framework are available?",

      "blocks": "nothing: the default proceeds"
    },
    {
      "id": "Q6",
      "category": "Delivery",
      "question": "Where should the service be delivered or deployed for use?",
      "changes": "Delivery steps and acceptance environment.",

  "summary": "S1 — Fact: deliver a small Python HTTP service in which organisers create seat-limited events and people reserve seats; the HTTP service is the named entry point and intended usable outcome. Assumptions: Q1–Q6 record the interaction, state, interface, runtime, and delivery defaults; in-memory state is lost on process exit, and anonymous access provides no privacy or authorization. Fact: this intake has an empty repository, no tools or files, no prior run, and no named deployment target; it implements nothing and grants no authority beyond the requested service. Discovery has no named team, workspace source, channel, internal site, document, private repository, owner, or additional ambiguous term as a source hint; if evidence becomes available later, discovery must first establish the runtime and delivery environment and any applicable product requirements before replacing the recorded defaults. A sensitive locator belongs only in an authorized private store, never in KNOWLEDGE/. The isolated source checkout remains at its snapshot until final return; the service becomes visible in the returned checkout then, and a deployed outcome exists only after release. S2 — Fact: include tests; assumption: use Python standard-library tests covering event creation, reservation capacity and concurrent requests, and error responses."
